client: I got laid off from my job at the marketing firm about a month ago, and honestly, I've been really struggling since then. The financial pressure is just constantly in the back of my mind, like this low hum of dread that never really goes away. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything practical, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help — that says a lot about your resilience. That "low hum of dread" you described is such a vivid way to capture how financial anxiety can sit with us constantly, and it makes complete sense that a month of that kind of pressure would feel exhausting and overwhelming. I'm curious — when that hum gets loudest, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, when it gets really loud, my mind just spirals into these worst-case scenarios — like I'll picture myself not being able to pay rent, losing my apartment, and somehow ending up completely alone with nothing. And then there's this voice that tells me I should have been smarter with money, that I made stupid decisions, and that I basically brought all of this on myself. It's like the anxiety and the guilt kind of feed each other, and I can't figure out which one starts it.
therapist: That spiral you're describing — where anxiety and guilt keep feeding each other — is incredibly common, and it makes sense your mind is doing that, even though it's so painful. I want to gently notice that the voice calling your decisions "stupid" is speaking with a lot of certainty, as if it has all the facts, but a sudden layoff involves so many factors completely outside your control. When that self-critical voice shows up, do you think it's being a fair witness to you — or is it holding you to a standard it wouldn't apply to someone else you cared about?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right — like, if a friend got laid off, I wouldn't tell them they were stupid for not seeing it coming. But when it's me, it just feels different, like the rules don't apply the same way. I guess I don't fully trust that voice of reason because the self-critical one is just so much louder and it's been there so much longer.
therapist: What you just named — that the self-critical voice feels louder because it's been there longer — is actually a really important insight, because it means that voice isn't necessarily *truer*, it's just more practiced. It's like a well-worn path in your mind that your thoughts automatically follow, while the kinder, more reasonable voice is a newer trail that takes more effort to find. What do you think that self-critical voice was originally trying to do for you — was there ever a time in your life when it felt like it was protecting you somehow?

client: That's... actually an interesting way to put it, the well-worn path thing. I think maybe the self-critical voice started as a way to stay ahead of other people's criticism — like if I tore myself down first, it hurt less when someone else did it. But I'm not sure "protecting" is the right word, because honestly it never really felt safe, it just felt like bracing for impact all the time.
therapist: "Bracing for impact" — that's such a honest and powerful way to describe it, and it actually reframes things meaningfully: this voice wasn't really keeping you safe, it was just making sure you were already hurting before anyone else could hurt you. That's an exhausting way to move through the world, and it makes a lot of sense that it developed, even if it's been costing you so much. I'm wondering — now that you can see it for what it is, a old defensive strategy rather than the truth about who you are, does that change how you feel toward that voice at all?

client: I mean... yeah, it does shift something a little, hearing it put that way. Like, I can almost feel sorry for that part of me, the part that figured out early on that if you expect the worst, at least you're not blindsided. But I'm also kind of skeptical, because understanding where it came from doesn't automatically make it quieter, you know?
therapist: That skepticism is completely valid and honestly quite wise — insight is a real first step, but it doesn't rewire a well-worn path overnight, and it would be unfair to suggest otherwise. What we're really talking about is gradually building that newer, kinder trail through small, repeated moments — like the one you just had, where you felt a flicker of compassion for that younger part of yourself instead of just believing what it says. I'm curious, in the past month, has there been even one small moment where you handled something in this difficult situation that, if you were being fair, you could acknowledge as a sign of your own strength?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to just say no. But... there was this one night last month where I was feeling really isolated and instead of just sitting there spiraling, I actually texted a friend, even though part of me was convinced she wouldn't want to hear from me. She did respond, and we ended up talking for a while, but I still kind of dismissed it afterward as not a big deal.
therapist: That moment is *exactly* the kind of thing worth pausing on, because what you did took real courage — you acted against the voice that said you'd be a burden, and it turned out that voice was wrong. And then notice what happened next: even when you got evidence that contradicted the self-critical story, you found a way to minimize it so the old narrative could stay intact. What do you think it would mean for you to actually let that moment count — to hold onto it as genuine proof of something?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but honestly it feels kind of dangerous to let that moment count too much. Like if I start thinking "okay, maybe I'm not a burden," and then the next time I reach out to someone they actually do pull away or seem annoyed, it'll hurt so much more than if I just kept my expectations low. I guess I've been protecting myself by not letting the good evidence stick, but I don't know if I'm ready to give that up.
therapist: You've just articulated something really profound — that keeping the good evidence from sticking isn't an accident, it's another form of that same "bracing for impact" strategy, a way of staying pre-hurt so the fall isn't as far. And I want to sit with that rather than rush past it, because you're not wrong that opening up to hope does carry some risk — but I'm wondering, how has the strategy of keeping expectations low actually been working for you, especially over this past month?

client: Honestly, it hasn't been working at all — I've just been walking around feeling kind of hollow, like I'm protecting myself from a fall that's already happening anyway. Keeping expectations low didn't stop the loneliness, it just made sure I had no reason to reach out or try, so I ended up more isolated than ever. I guess I thought it was smart, like armor, but it's starting to feel more like a cage.
therapist: "Armor that became a cage" — that's one of the most honest and courageous things you could recognize about yourself, and the fact that you can see it so clearly right now feels like something genuinely significant. You came in today doubting that talking could change anything practical, and while we haven't solved the financial pressure, you've uncovered something that's been quietly running your life for a long time. I'm wondering — given everything you've just realized, what might one small, low-stakes experiment look like this week, something that lets you test ever so slightly whether the cage door might open?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true — that recognizing the pattern is actually meaningful. But when you ask about a "small experiment," my brain immediately goes to all the reasons it won't work, like what if I let someone in a little and they use it against me, or what if I look weak at work right now when I really can't afford to? I guess the honest answer is I don't even know what a low-stakes moment would look like anymore, because everything feels high-stakes when money is this tight.
therapist: It makes complete sense that when survival feels threatened, the nervous system stops being able to distinguish between big risks and small ones — everything gets flagged as dangerous, so of course "low-stakes" feels like a foreign concept right now. I want to honor that rather than push past it, because the goal isn't to talk you into feeling safe when you genuinely aren't feeling that way. I'm wondering though — is there one person in your life, maybe even the friend you texted, where the trust already exists enough that "letting them in a little" wouldn't feel like handing them a weapon, but more like... just not pretending everything is fine?

client: I mean... maybe. There's this one friend, Dara, who I texted a few weeks ago when things felt really bad, and she didn't freak out or try to fix everything, she just said "I'm here." But even thinking about going back to her now feels like too much, like I used up my one moment of vulnerability and if I go back again she's going to think I'm too much to handle.
therapist: That thought — "I used up my one moment of vulnerability" — is worth looking at closely, because it's treating Dara's care like a limited resource that runs out, rather than something she offered freely and has likely meant. And notice that when she said "I'm here," she didn't put a number on it. I'm curious — if Dara came back to you a second time during a hard stretch in her life, would you find yourself thinking "she's too much," or would reaching out again actually feel like she trusted you?
